title: JC H2 chemistry — inorganic: periodicity, groups and transition metals
subject: science

scenes.caption: Across period 3, atoms shrink
scenes.narration: Across period 3, from sodium to argon, each atom holds its outer electrons tighter. Follow the probe: the same electron shell, pulled ever closer.

shape.explain: Sodium (Na): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Magnesium (Mg): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Aluminium (Al): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Silicon (Si): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Phosphorus (P): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Sulphur (S): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Chlorine (Cl): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
Argon (Ar): period 3 atom, drawn smaller than the last — atomic radius shrinks across the period.
The probe: follow it left to right and watch every atom get smaller.
The shrinking trend: atomic radius falls from sodium to argon as nuclear charge rises.

scenes.caption: Melting point tells the structure story
scenes.narration: Melting point follows structure, not just size. It climbs through the metals, peaks at silicon's giant covalent lattice, then falls away for the simple molecular elements.

shape.explain: Sodium: a metal — its bar stages in at a modest melting point.
Magnesium: a metal with stronger metallic bonding, so a taller bar.
Aluminium: a metal — watch its bar grow to full height.
Silicon: giant covalent lattice — watch its bar climb to the peak.
Phosphorus: a simple molecular element — only weak forces between molecules, so a short bar.
Sulphur: a simple molecular element — only weak forces between molecules, so a short bar.
Chlorine: a simple molecular element — only weak forces between molecules, so a short bar.
Argon: a simple molecular element — only weak forces between molecules, so a short bar.
The probe travels the melting-point trend: up through the metals, peaking at silicon, then falling away.

scenes.caption: First ionisation energy: the rise, and two dips
scenes.narration: First ionisation energy generally rises across the period — but it dips at aluminium and again at sulphur. The probe dips where a 3p electron, or a paired 3p electron, is easier to remove.

shape.explain: Sodium (Na): first ionisation energy plotted as height.
Magnesium (Mg): first ionisation energy plotted as height.
Aluminium (Al): first ionisation energy plotted as height — the dip: its 3p electron is easier to remove.
Silicon (Si): first ionisation energy plotted as height.
Phosphorus (P): first ionisation energy plotted as height.
Sulphur (S): first ionisation energy plotted as height — the dip: its 3p electron is easier to remove.
Argon (Ar): first ionisation energy plotted as height.
The probe draws the ionisation-energy curve: rising overall, dipping twice.

scenes.caption: Down group 2: reactivity climbs
scenes.narration: Down group 2, reactivity climbs. Each chip drops into the column while the reactivity bar grows — strontium reacts far more violently than beryllium.

shape.explain: Beryllium (Be): a group 2 metal — watch it drop into its slot down the column.
Magnesium (Mg): a group 2 metal — watch it drop into its slot down the column.
Calcium (Ca): a group 2 metal — watch it drop into its slot down the column.
Strontium (Sr): a group 2 metal — watch it drop into its slot down the column.
The reactivity bar: it grows taller as the chips land further down the group.

scenes.caption: Down group 17: oxidising power falls
scenes.narration: Down group 17, oxidising power falls. The halogen chips drop down the group while the oxidising-strength gauge drains — fluorine is fierce, iodine is mild.

shape.explain: Fluorine (F): a halogen — watch it drop into its slot down the group.
Chlorine (Cl): a halogen — watch it drop into its slot down the group.
Bromine (Br): a halogen — watch it drop into its slot down the group.
Iodine (I): a halogen — watch it drop into its slot down the group.
The oxidising-strength gauge: full for fluorine, draining as the chips land lower.

scenes.caption: Colour comes from partially filled d-orbitals
scenes.narration: Colour in transition metal ions comes from partially filled d-orbitals. Copper(II) is 3d9 — the blue ring appears — while zinc(II) is 3d10, full and colourless.

shape.explain: d-orbital box 1 of 3: each box holds up to two d-electrons.
d-orbital box 2 of 3: each box holds up to two d-electrons.
d-orbital box 3 of 3: each box holds up to two d-electrons.
Copper(II): a 3d9 ion — watch it travel into the d-orbital diagram.
d-electron 1: staged into the boxes — the subshell fills but stays partial.
d-electron 2: staged into the boxes — the subshell fills but stays partial.
d-electron 3: staged into the boxes — the subshell fills but stays partial.
The colour appears: 3d9 is partially filled, so copper(II) is blue.
Zinc(II): a 3d10 ion — watch it travel in beside copper.

scenes.caption: Ligands crowd the metal; catalysts flip oxidation states
scenes.narration: Ligands crowd around the metal centre to form a complex. In the contact process the vanadium catalyst flips between oxidation states — and comes back unchanged.

shape.explain: The metal centre: ligands crowd around it to form a complex.

Ligand 3: a lone-pair donor — watch it travel into its slot around the metal.
Ligand 4: a lone-pair donor — watch it travel into its slot around the metal.
The catalyst's oxidation state: watch it flip as the reaction cycles.

scenes.caption: A common mistake: zinc is a transition metal
scenes.narration: A common mistake: zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block. But zinc(II) has a full 3d subshell — five full pairs, no colour, no variable oxidation states — so zinc is not a transition metal.

shape.explain: Zinc: it sits in the d-block — but is it a transition metal?

steps.text: A common mistake: zinc is a transition metal

shape.explain: 3d electron pair 1 of 5: the subshell fills completely — nothing partial left.
3d electron pair 2 of 5: the subshell fills completely — nothing partial left.
3d electron pair 3 of 5: the subshell fills completely — nothing partial left.
3d electron pair 4 of 5: the subshell fills completely — nothing partial left.
3d electron pair 5 of 5: the subshell fills completely — nothing partial left.
Iron(II): a true transition metal ion — watch it travel in for contrast.
The colour appears on iron only: partially filled d-orbitals give colour and variable oxidation states.
